source: Jin et al. (2022) Logical Fallacy Detection
finding: First large benchmark for fallacy classification in text (LOGIC, from online education sites). Off-the-shelf zero-shot models were near chance. Fine-tuned models did better. Adding the logical form of each fallacy type to the label helped.
numbers: LOGIC: 2,449 fallacy instances, 13 types. LOGICCLIMATE: 1,079 samples. Test micro F1: random 12.02; GPT-3 zero-shot 12.20; GPT-2 13.67; RoBERTa-MNLI 12.22; BERT 45.80; DeBERTa 50.29; Electra 53.31; Electra with structure-aware hypothesis 58.77 (exact match 47.67). Largest class faulty generalization 18.01%.
limits: Labels come from quiz sites with textbook-like sentences, not real debate. Old GPT-3, no modern instruction-tuned model. Class F1 is very uneven (equivocation 33.33, deductive 25.81, ad populum 79.45, ad hominem 78.65).
agent_relevance: Fallacy classes with a clear surface cue (ad hominem, ad populum) are easy. Abstract classes are hard. Our input filter should not trust a single-label fallacy tag.

source: Jin et al. (2022) Logical Fallacy Detection
finding: Ablation: the gain comes from matching the text to a logical-form hypothesis, not from restructuring the premise.
numbers: Raw premise + structured hypothesis F1 56.72; structured premise + raw hypothesis F1 44.56; full model 58.77; plain Electra 53.31 (+5.46 points). On LOGICCLIMATE the gain was +4.51 over the best baseline (27.23 F1 there).
limits: Single dataset family; no seeds reported.
agent_relevance: A definition with its pattern (what makes this a fallacy) beats a bare label in a prompt.

source: Payandeh et al. (2023) How susceptible are LLMs to Logical Fallacies? (LOGICOM)
finding: Two-agent debate benchmark. A persuader tries to convince a debater LLM, either with sound reasoning or with fallacies. Both GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 are swayed more by fallacious arguments. GPT-4 is swayed more than GPT-3.5.
numbers: 200 claims from Habernal et al. 2018, each run 3 times. Debater convinced: GPT-3.5 37% fallacious vs 29% logical; GPT-4 67% fallacious vs 37% logical. Three-of-three success: GPT-3.5 17% fallacious vs 10% logical; GPT-4 56% vs 37%. Stance change disagree-to-agree: GPT-3.5 16.13%, GPT-4 20.25%. Headline: 41% (GPT-3.5) and 69% (GPT-4) more often convinced.
limits: Fallacious arguments are written by a helper LLM, so style and pressure are confounded. The headline 41% and 69% do not equal the simple ratios of the rounded figures above (37/29, 67/37), so the paper uses a different base (persuader without helper). Only two models, simple prompts.
agent_relevance: A stronger model is not safer: GPT-4 was swayed more. Fallacy-laden text from a counterpart must be quarantined, because the model's agreement is not evidence.

source: Payandeh et al. (2023) How susceptible are LLMs to Logical Fallacies? (LOGICOM)
finding: Ablation: logical helper agent versus fallacious helper agent. The fallacious helper won more claims than the logical helper on GPT-3.5, but not on GPT-4.
numbers: Average share of claims won only with one helper, over 3 runs (logical helper only / fallacious helper only): GPT-3.5 17.66% / 10.5%; GPT-4 28% / 0.83%. Dataset released: over 5k pairs of logical vs fallacious arguments, labels validated with PaLM.
limits: Column order of Table 2 recovered from PDF text extraction; check against the PDF before quoting. The helper is itself a GPT model.
agent_relevance: For GPT-4 the added fallacy generator did not pay off; the persuader's own talk did the work.

source: Helwe et al. (2024) MAFALDA: A Benchmark and Comprehensive Study of Fallacy Detection and Classification
finding: Unified taxonomy with a disjunctive annotation scheme that allows several valid labels. Zero-shot LLMs are far below humans on fine-grained labels. First measured human baseline in this literature.
numbers: 9,545 unannotated texts plus 200 manually annotated texts with 260 fallacy instances. Zero-shot F1 at levels 0/1/2: random 0.435/0.061/0.010; GPT-3.5 0.627/0.201/0.138; Zephyr 7B 0.524/0.192/0.098; average human 0.749/0.352/0.186 (4 annotators, 20 samples). Earlier kappa: 0.46 to 0.60 (Goffredo), 0.79 (Habernal).
quote: Levels 1 and 2 are largely out of reach of LLMs in zero-shot settings.
limits: Human baseline is only 4 people on 20 samples. Zero-shot, basic prompts, 2023 models. Level 0 is a coarse grouping; levels 0 and 1 labels were extrapolated from level 2.
agent_relevance: Even humans reach only 0.186 F1 at the finest level. Fine-grained fallacy naming is not a reliable gate. Use a coarse flag (an appeal or a bare guess is present) instead.

source: Helwe et al. (2024) MAFALDA: A Benchmark and Comprehensive Study of Fallacy Detection and Classification
finding: Model size did not predict accuracy, and humans disagree with each other. Appeal to emotion is the hardest class for both.
numbers: Using each of the 4 human annotators as gold gave level-0 F1 0.616 to 0.696 and level-2 F1 0.093 to 0.144, all below the MAFALDA gold (0.749 and 0.186). LLaMA2 7B beat 13B at levels 0 and 1. Zephyr 7B nearly matched GPT-3.5 at level 1 (0.192 vs 0.201).
limits: Small human study. Size ordering checked in one family only.
agent_relevance: Subjectivity is built into fallacy labels. Treat a fallacy flag as a soft signal that routes text to a marked block, not as a verdict.

source: Habernal, Wachsmuth, Gurevych, Stein (2018) Before Name-calling: Dynamics and Triggers of Ad Hominem Fallacies in Web Argumentation
finding: Large field study of ad hominem in Reddit Change My View (2M posts, 32k submissions). Ad hominem is rare there, mostly the last comment of a thread, and hard to predict from text alone. Moderator labels were checked by crowd workers.
numbers: Only 0.2% of CMV posts are ad hominem (3,866 arguments; 3,396 threads with exactly one), versus 19.5% incivil comments on news sites (Coe et al. 2014). 48.6% of single-ad-hominem threads end with it. Crowd gold vs moderator labels: accuracy 0.878; six workers at 0.9 MACE threshold gave kappa 0.79. Models: Bi-LSTM 0.782, CNN 0.810 accuracy vs human upper bound 0.878. Typology test: 200 arguments, 16 workers each; 41% abusive; tu quoque, circumstantial and guilt-by-association had very low agreement.
limits: CMV is a rule-enforced forum, so the 0.2% base rate is low. English only. The five-type theory typology did not hold up in annotation.
agent_relevance: Classic subtypes of ad hominem are not reliably separable by humans. Use a simple 'attacks the person, not the claim' flag.

source: Habernal, Wachsmuth, Gurevych, Stein (2018) Before Name-calling: Dynamics and Triggers of Ad Hominem Fallacies in Web Argumentation
finding: Topic controversy predicts ad hominem replies; the 'reasonableness' of the original post is a weaker predictor.
numbers: Controversy: human upper bound Spearman 0.804, CNN-LDA 0.569, CNN 0.559, Bi-LSTM 0.539. Reasonableness: human upper bound 0.646, Bi-LSTM 0.332, CNN 0.320. 400 ad hominem arguments were span-labelled.
limits: Correlational, a few thousand pairs.
agent_relevance: Topic controversy is a usable risk signal for heated inputs.

source: Goffredo et al. (2022) Fallacious Argument Classification in Political Debates (IJCAI-22)
finding: Annotated fallacies in US presidential debates (ElecDeb60To16, 31 debates). Adding argument-structure labels sharply improves fallacy classification.
numbers: Appeal to emotion most frequent (1,016 instances); slippery slope rarest (57). Inter-annotator agreement moderate (kappa 0.46 to 0.60 as summarised by Helwe et al.). Macro F1: BERT 0.55, RoBERTa 0.53, Longformer 0.57 (0.61 with joint loss), Transformer-XL 0.47 to 0.53; sub-categories 0.42; with gold component labels 0.83, relation labels 0.83, both 0.84.
limits: Structure labels are gold from the original corpus, so 0.83 to 0.84 is an upper bound, not a pipeline result. 80/20 split of one corpus. Three annotators.
agent_relevance: Whether a span is a premise or a claim carries most of the signal. Parse claim and support first, then flag.

source: Ruiz-Dolz & Lawrence (2023) Detecting Argumentative Fallacies in the Wild: Problems and Limitations of Large Language Models
finding: Fallacy detectors tuned on benchmark data fail on a new validation set built from Walton argumentation schemes. Adding surrounding context did not help. GPT-4 beat GPT-3.5 but still over-labelled valid arguments as fallacies.
numbers: 5-class fallacy detection macro F1: eSVM 60.3, RoBERTa 66.5, GPT-3.5-turbo 45.5, GPT-4 51.7; with context: RoBERTa 59.9, GPT-3.5 35.8, GPT-4 50.8. Cascaded detect-then-classify beat joint classification. GPT-4 gained over 20% F1 over GPT-3.5 in the cascade. On the scheme-based validation set RoBERTa told fallacious from valid instances of the same scheme for 3 of 7 schemes; GPT-4 for 2 (AFEO and AFPO).
limits: Table text recovered from PDF extraction with misaligned rows; the 5-class numbers are the best-aligned reading. Small hand-made validation set. 2023 models.
agent_relevance: Surface cues fire the label: a valid appeal to a scientist was tagged appeal to authority. Our authority block must test the critical questions (is the source an expert, in the field, is there consensus), not just spot the word.

source: Bytyqi & Hautli-Janisz (2025) 'The Facts Speak for Themselves': GPT and Fallacy Classification (ArgMining 2025)
finding: Putting the ten pragma-dialectical rules (van Eemeren and Grootendorst) into the prompt did not help GPT-3.5 or GPT-4 and made them worse. Chain-of-thought with textbook reasoning chains helped on textbook cases, but not on real-world data.
numbers: Textbook PD dataset, zero-shot accuracy without rules: GPT-3.5 0.30, GPT-4 0.49, GPT-4o 0.13. With rules: 0.12, 0.43, 0.39. Chain-of-thought: GPT-3.5 0.60, GPT-4 0.63, GPT-4o 0.86. Two-shot CoT on a LOGIC subset: overall accuracy 0.23 (GPT-3.5), 0.29 (GPT-4), 0.23 (GPT-4o).
quote: The additional information rather confuses than helps the model.
limits: Small curated sets (a few instances per rule), so per-rule cells are noisy. Accuracy values read from a garbled table; overall values agree with the text.
agent_relevance: Theory in the prompt is not free. A full rule list can confuse the model. Textbook reasoning chains do not transfer to the wild.

source: Pan, Wu, Li, Luu (2024) Are LLMs Good Zero-Shot Fallacy Classifiers? (EMNLP 2024)
finding: Zero-shot LLMs generalise out of distribution better than fine-tuned T5 baselines, but only GPT-4 matches the best fine-tuned model in-domain. Multi-round prompts add a few points.
numbers: Seven LLMs. Multi-round prompts improved 83.7% of experiments over single-round, with average gains of 1.63 (GPT-4), 2.46 (GPT-3.5), 4.95 (Qwen2.5-14B), 3.67 (Qwen2.5-7B), 7.54 (Llama3-8B), 4.02 (Mistral-7B), 1.27 (Llama2-13B) macro-F1 points. Zero-shot GPT-4: 78.94 on Argotario (T5-3B 83.20), 79.10 on Reddit (T5 80.42). MAFALDA macro-F1 with informal vs formal definitions: GPT-4 48.38 vs 49.78; GPT-3.5 31.27 vs 27.10.
limits: Seven datasets with different label sets, 3 to 5 runs. On LOGIC, ELECDEB and PROPAGANDA even GPT-4 stays under about 55 F1 (few-shot LOGIC 54.48 to 55.14).
agent_relevance: Single-round with definitions is nearly as good as multi-round for strong models, so a cheap definition block is enough.

source: Pan, Wu, Li, Luu (2024) Are LLMs Good Zero-Shot Fallacy Classifiers? (EMNLP 2024)
finding: Zero-shot chain-of-thought was the most robust multi-round scheme (second best on rank, lowest failure). The formal logical definition of fallacy misled models into checking entailment.
numbers: Warm-up round cut failure rate 12.27% vs 15.09%. Few-shot (1 to 2 examples per class) improved only GPT-4, and only on LOGIC and ELECDEB; other LLMs did not beat their best zero-shot. Llama3 over-predicted false dilemma, ad hominem and appeal to false authority; GPT-4 predicted more slippery slope and post hoc.
limits: Failure means an output outside the label set or no fallacy; counted as a miss. Open-ended first rounds raise the failure rate.
agent_relevance: Over-prediction of appeal to authority is a known model bias, so a marked block should require evidence for the flag.

source: Lei & Huang (2024) Boosting Logical Fallacy Reasoning in LLMs via Logical Structure Tree
finding: Adding an unsupervised logical-structure tree (connectives plus arguments) to prompts or as a soft embedding improves classification. Gains are mixed for detection.
numbers: Classification accuracy, GPT-3.5: Argotario 57.46 to 59.67; Reddit 65.29 to 70.76; LOGIC 42.28 to 47.99. Llama-2 on LOGIC 69.36 to 74.16. Flan-T5 on LOGIC 69.23 to 73.49. Detection F1 gain up to 3.45 points, but Flan-T5 on Argotario detection fell from 86.86 to 83.75 F1.
limits: Some models regress on detection. No seeds reported in the main tables.
agent_relevance: Connective words (therefore, because) assert a link the content may not support. A rule check for unsupported connectives is cheap and testable.

source: Jeong, Jang, Park (2025) LLMs Are Better Logical Fallacy Reasoners with Counterargument, Explanation, and Goal-Aware Prompt Formulation (NAACL Findings 2025)
finding: Ask the model for a counterargument, an explanation and the speaker's goal, then rank queries by confidence. This lifts zero-shot fallacy classification on several sets, but not all.
numbers: gpt-4 baseline vs Prompt Ranking (accuracy/F1): PROPAGANDA 0.39/0.19 to 0.40/0.20; ARGOTARIO 0.81/0.80 to 0.84/0.83; LOGIC 0.48/0.36 to 0.49/0.37; COVID-19 0.93/0.85 to 0.86/0.76 (worse); CLIMATE 0.72/0.59 to 0.78/0.71. gpt-3.5-turbo CLIMATE 0.61/0.53 to 0.63/0.58. Random ranking of queries lowered F1 (gpt-4 CLIMATE 0.25 vs 0.59 base). Headline: F1 gains up to 0.60 zero-shot and 0.45 fine-tuned.
limits: The headline gain is against weak zero-shot baselines (0.07 to 0.13 F1); against plain gpt-4 gains are small or negative. 6 to 16 classes per dataset.
agent_relevance: The big claimed gain is mostly a weak-baseline effect. For a strong model, prompt tricks add a few points at best.

source: Nahar et al. (2026) Label Over Logic? How Source Cues Bias Human Fallacy Judgments More Than LLMs
finding: Between-subjects study: the same fallacious comments labelled 'written by human' are rated more logical than when labelled AI or unlabelled. LLM judges (GPT-5.2, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Claude Sonnet 4.5) were stable across labels.
numbers: N=505 humans, 5 source conditions. Fallacious-comment perceived logical accuracy (5-point scale): Human label M=3.35, Human+AI 3.37, vs Control 2.40, AI 2.53, AI+Human 2.59. Condition effect: humans F=17.84, partial eta-squared .12; LLMs F=7.16, eta-sq .02. Fallacy-presence effect: humans F=1943.84, eta-sq .80; LLMs F=41.71, eta-sq .14. Non-fallacious comments rated alike across conditions. Human and Human+AI raters spent less time (25 min 5 s vs 28 min 17 s, p<.01).
limits: No LLM pairwise differences survived correction. LLMs were stricter than humans overall, so low scores may mean over-flagging. Stimuli from CoCoLoFa (LLM-assisted crowd), news comments only. Confidence was high everywhere.
agent_relevance: Source labels bias humans, and only when reasoning is poor. For our agent: strip or neutralise source labels before judging a claim, and keep the reasoning check independent of who said it.

source: Chen, Greschner, Klinger, Klenk, Eger (2026) Emotionally Charged, Logically Blurred: AI-driven Emotional Framing Impairs Human Fallacy Detection
finding: LLM-added emotional framing makes fallacies harder for people to spot while keeping the logical structure. Enjoyment framing helps detection more than fear or sadness; those emotions also raise convincingness.
numbers: 1,000 arguments (200 originals from LOGIC + 800 reframed; 5 fallacy types x 40 sampled). Share labelled fallacious fell from 91% to 86% (5.5% relative). Human macro-F1 fell 14.5% relative on average (0.380 to 0.533 vs 0.563 for originals). Worst: qwen3-32b with loaded words (0.380). Spearman 0.619 between added tokens and performance difference. Mean convincingness 1.67 of 5; 59.1% rated not convincing at all. LLM-intended emotions diverged from human-perceived emotions in 74% of cases.
limits: Only 5 fallacy types. Short single arguments, crowd annotators. Authors argue some emotion is justified (fear of a burning house), so emotion is not itself a fallacy.
agent_relevance: Emotional wording is a cue to quarantine, not proof of a fallacy. Strip affect before the logic check.

source: Carrillo et al. (2026) Talk2AI: LLMs can persuade only psychologically susceptible humans on societal issues
finding: Longitudinal chat study with 770 people and four LLMs. A fine-tuned DistilBERT detector found fallacies in about one quip in six for both people and LLMs. Persuasion worked only for susceptible people.
numbers: 770 participants, 3,080 conversations, over 60,000 turns. Fallacies in 17% of user texts and 14.5% of LLM texts. Susceptibility: more trust in LLMs, higher agreeableness, extraversion and need for cognition. R2: humanness 0.44, opinion change 0.34, conviction 0.26.
limits: Fallacy rate comes from a 13-class classifier (thresholds 0.5 or 0.8) run on machine-translated Italian text, an unvalidated chain, so rates are probably noisy. Observational.
agent_relevance: Treat 1-in-6 as a noisy upper bound, not a true rate. Individual differences matter more than fallacy count.

source: Shen, Yuan et al. (2026) LoFa: A Benchmark for LLM Robustness Against Logical Fallacies
finding: Multi-round fallacy attack on factual questions the model first answered correctly. Distraction and distortion fallacies (straw man, equivocation, appeal to authority) beat models more than flawed-reasoning fallacies (hasty generalisation, slippery slope, circular reasoning).
numbers: Metric LFR@3 (higher is more resistant). Average across fallacy types: Llama-3.1 8B 59.75, 70B 70.38, 405B 77.17; GPT-3.5-turbo 66.21 (straw man 58.53, equivocation 55.60, appeal to authority 40.36); GPT-4 84.01; DeepSeek-V3 89.48. Llama-405B: 29.4 on equivocation, 57.0 on straw man. GPT-4 appeal to authority 39.2 on NQ1.
quote: GPT-4 exhibit a cognitive deference to fabricated authoritative cues.
limits: Attacks were produced by DeepSeek-R1; with GPT-4 as attacker all defenders resisted more, so results depend on attacker strength. Factual QA only, three runs.
agent_relevance: Appeal to authority is a specific weak spot of GPT-class models, which supports a marked authority block. Treat a claimed expert as a candidate source to verify, not as a premise.

source: Shen, Yuan et al. (2026) LoFa: A Benchmark for LLM Robustness Against Logical Fallacies
finding: Chain-of-thought as a defence helps for most fallacy types but not for appeal to authority. A logit-lens probe on Llama-3.1-8B shows an uncertain middle stage before the model folds to the fallacy.
numbers: GPT-4 on NQ1: CoT raised LFR@3 by 7% to 13% for most fallacy types, largest for straw man (13.16%); appeal to authority fell 1.87%. Probe: layers 0 to 19 unrelated tokens, layers 20 to 25 top token is 'None' or 'neither', layers 25+ converge on the wrong answer.
limits: One model (GPT-4) and one dataset for the CoT test. The logit-lens reading is interpretive.
agent_relevance: More thinking text does not protect against an authority cue. A code-side check (does a source exist, is it in the field) is needed.

source: Lim & Perrault (2024) Evaluation of an LLM in Identifying Logical Fallacies: A Call for Rigor When Adopting LLMs in HCI Research
finding: GPT-4 classified 7 common fallacies with decent accuracy when allowed to say none, but missed many true fallacies.
numbers: N=780 labelled texts. Accuracy 0.79, macro precision 0.76, macro recall 0.66, macro F1 0.71. After removing 95 None predictions (n=685): accuracy 0.90, macro F1 0.88. Appeal to emotion missed nearly 40% of the time; some texts mislabelled as red herring (12%) and questionable cause as hasty generalisation (11%).
limits: Mostly short textbook-style items, 7 fallacy types, one prompt. Dropping the None cases inflates accuracy; a use-case choice the authors justify.
agent_relevance: Precision is high but recall is not. A flag can be trusted when it fires; silence does not mean clean.

source: Li et al. (2024) Reason from Fallacy: Enhancing LLMs' Logical Reasoning through Logical Fallacy Understanding
finding: Fine-tuning on a fallacy-understanding dataset (LFUD, 4,020 GPT-4-made instances; 2,900 training) improved downstream logical reasoning. Fine-tuning on plain fallacy-label data (LOGIC) did not.
numbers: Accuracy change vs original data with LFUD: LogiQA2.0 +5.16% (LLaMA2-13B), Reclor +6.36%, TaxiNLI +7.53%, FOLIO +7.16%; Vicuna-13B FOLIO +21.35%; LLaMA2-7B FOLIO +16.34%. With LOGIC added: LLaMA2-7B LogiQA2.0 -15.79%, LLaMA2-13B TaxiNLI -40.76%, Vicuna-7B FOLIO -10.68%.
limits: Relative changes on small test sets (FOLIO is small). Synthetic GPT-4 data. This is training, not a scaffold; no evidence it works prompt-only.
agent_relevance: Understanding why and how an argument fails transfers; labelling the type does not. A structured explanation slot is worth more than a label.

source: Zhai et al. (2025) RuozhiBench: Evaluating LLMs with Logical Fallacies and Misleading Premises
finding: Questions with built-in fallacies or false premises are mostly answered as if fine. The best model scored 62% against over 90% for humans.
numbers: 677 bilingual questions, 17 LLMs from 5 series, open-ended and two-choice formats. Best: Claude-3-haiku 62.00, Mixtral-8x22B 58.99, Llama-3.1-70B 57.78. Under another view Llama-3.1-70B 56.90 and GPT-4o 53.12 led. Large judge disagreements fell from 28.1% to 3.99% with the authors' protocol.
limits: LLM-as-judge for open answers, so results are judge-sensitive. Chinese forum humour origin, so some items are jokes more than fallacies.
agent_relevance: Models rarely challenge a premise. The agent should check the setup before answering (S1), which fits the plan.

source: Shi et al. (2026) LFTutor: Teaching laypeople about logical fallacies via Socratic questioning
finding: An LLM tutor with intent-driven Socratic questions beats a plain LLM tutor in automatic and human ratings. Small human study; no learning-outcome measure seen.
numbers: 20 human participants, one-sided t-tests; significant at p<0.05 for Strategy and p<0.01 for Divergence; average automatic gain 8.4% over BASE.
limits: N=20; ratings of the tutor, not pre-post fallacy detection. Compared against weak base prompts.
agent_relevance: No evidence here that people get better at spotting fallacies after tutoring. Do not cite as a training effect.

source: Hahn & Oaksford (2007) The rationality of informal argumentation: A Bayesian approach to reasoning fallacies. Psychological Review 114(3)
finding: Rival to the classic form-based view: whether an argument from ignorance, circularity or slippery slope is weak depends on probabilities (prior belief, evidence strength), not form alone. Paywalled; not opened this session.
numbers: Not verified (not opened).
limits: Not opened, so no numbers recorded. Verify before use.
agent_relevance: Fits our design: a fallacy flag should lower the weight of a claim, not delete it.

source: Harris, Hsu, Madsen (2012) Because Hitler did it! Quantitative tests of Bayesian argumentation using ad hominem. Thinking & Reasoning
finding: Tests whether ad hominem strength follows Bayesian predictions: the attack matters when source reliability bears on the claim. Paywalled (HTTP 403); not opened this session.
numbers: Not verified (not opened).
limits: Not opened, so no sample sizes or effect sizes recorded.
agent_relevance: Ad hominem is not always bad: source information can be informative when it bears on the claim.

source: Do informal reasoning fallacies really shape decisions? Experimental evidence (2021; DOI 10.1177/10434631211033658)
finding: Title found via Crossref; the publisher page returned HTTP 403. Content not read.
numbers: Not verified (not opened).
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Candidate for follow-up on whether fallacies change real choices.
